title: Nyaya (logic)
hook: a bank teller holds a note up to the light, and Nyaya teaches you to do the same with a reason

segments.voice: Yesterday in Nyaya, logic: three kinds of talk. Vada wants to find out, jalpa wants to win, vitanda only knocks down. Halfway through a disagreement, did you catch which one you were in? Day one thousand one hundred sixty-four.

At the bank counter, a teller takes a large note from a customer, and before she counts it she does something quick and almost unconscious. She holds it up to the light. She's not accusing anybody. She just knows that some notes look exactly like money and aren't. The color is right, the size is right, the number in the corner is right, and still there's nothing behind it. The Nyaya Sutra thinks reasons are like that. Some reasons are real. Some only look like reasons. And it gives the look-alikes a name, so you can learn to hold them up to the light.
screen: `A NOTE HELD UP TO THE LIGHT.` → `LOOKS LIKE MONEY, ISN'T.` → `SOME REASONS ARE LIKE THAT.`

segments.voice: The name is hetvabhasa. Hetu is the reason, the second of the five parts we met two days ago. On the ridge with the smoke, we brushed past this idea; today it gets its own day. Abhasa is a semblance, a likeness, a thing that shines like something it isn't. So a hetvabhasa is a reason that only looks like one. The Nyaya Sutra lists five of them. Here are three, in everyday clothes. The first is the wandering reason. It shows up where your conclusion is true, but it also shows up where it isn't, so it can't carry you anywhere. This restaurant must be good, because it's crowded. But crowds also gather where food is cheap, or new, or the only place open late. The reason wanders. The second is the contradicting reason, which turns around and proves the opposite of what you wanted. I can't be a beginner at this, because I keep making beginner's mistakes. The third is the reason that still needs proving itself. It stands in the same spot as the claim, as unproved as what it was meant to prove. This plan will work, because it's a good plan. The note looks fine, but there's nothing behind it. Nyaya didn't keep this list to score points in debate. In the Sutra's own opening, getting free of false knowledge is tied to the highest good, and a false reason is one of the quietest ways false knowledge gets in. So the habit it asks for is simple, and a little humbling. Hold your own reasons up to the light first, before anyone else's.
screen: `HETVABHASA: A LOOK-ALIKE REASON.` · `THE WANDERING REASON.` · `THE REASON THAT FLIPS ON YOU.` · `THE REASON THAT NEEDS PROVING TOO.` · then, large: `HOLD YOUR OWN UP TO THE LIGHT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold one reason up to the light. Settle, and breathe out slowly a few times. Bring to mind something you've told yourself lately with a "because" in it. I'm bad at this, because. They don't care, because. It won't work out, because. Say the reason quietly, and then turn it over. Does it wander, showing up just as often when the opposite is true? Does it flip, pointing the other way? Does it need proving as much as the thing it holds up? You don't have to fix it. Just look. Then let it go, and rest with the breath. If you pray, you can offer the reason up and let it be seen by a clearer light than yours. The bell holds the time.
Nyaya. Today, its hetvabhasa: the reason that only looks like a reason, and the habit of checking your own first.
Your line: Nyaya, logic. Today, catch one "because" in your own head and hold it up to the light. Does it wander, flip, or need proving? Day one thousand one hundred sixty-four.

howItsDone: Students of Nyaya learn the hetvabhasas, the kinds of false reason, as part of the Nyaya Sutra's teaching, and use them to test arguments in discussion with a teacher.

original.note: Sanskrit: hetvabhasa, from hetu, a reason, and abhasa, a semblance: a false reason.

trapdoor: what you thought: a bad argument is just a wrong one.
what it means: some reasons only look like reasons. Nyaya names them so you can catch them, starting with your own.
what a scholar hears: Nyaya Sutra 1.2.4–9 lists five hetvabhasas, among them savyabhichara, the wandering reason, and viruddha, the contradicting one.
recall: a saying: Akka Mahadevi's short free poems

sources.ref: Nyaya Sutra 1.1.1–2 (knowledge of the categories and the removal of false knowledge lead to the highest good)

notes: Editor pass: acknowledged that 1161 touched false reasons in passing; replaced the 'she's quiet, so she's angry' example (third day running of reading someone's silence) with a crowded restaurant; removed the stock 'ordinary Tuesday' line.

Nyaya Sutra 1.2.4 lists five hetvabhasas (savyabhichara, viruddha, prakaranasama, sadhyasama, kalatita); 1.2.5–9 define them. Three are explained with the writer's own everyday examples (not from the text): confirm that 'the reason that still needs proving' fairly renders sadhyasama, and that the 'beginner's mistakes' example works for viruddha.
Hetvabhasa glossed as hetu + abhasa ('semblance'); standard lexicon sense, confirm.
The tie between false knowledge and the highest good is paraphrased from Nyaya Sutra 1.1.1–2; 1165 develops this chain more fully.
